title: Using the froe for riving
subtitle: The core splitting technique for green woodwork
excerpt: Riving is the technique of splitting wood along the grain with a froe and mallet. It produces pieces that follow the natural fibre direction, which are stronger than sawn equivalents. This technique underpins almost all green woodwork: chair legs, rake handles, basket stakes, and cleft fencing.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cleaving tool with a blade set at right angles to its handle. Struck with a mallet to split wood along the grain.
Splitting wood along the grain using a froe and mallet rather than sawing across it. Riven surfaces follow the grain and are stronger than sawn surfaces.
Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.

content.text: Riving
is splitting wood with the grain using a
froe

and mallet. The split follows the fibres of the wood rather than crossing them, which produces a surface that is stronger than a sawn surface of the same dimensions. What makes riving work is that wood fibres are more easily separated from each other along their length than they are broken across it.
The technique is used in
green wood

because the fibres of green wood separate easily. Dry wood can be split but requires more force and the split is less predictable. The ideal material is a straight-grained section cut within the past two weeks.
Before you start.
Never strike the cutting edge of the froe. Strike the spine (the back, thickened edge). Striking the cutting edge will roll or chip it.
Stand the log section on a stable chopping block. A rolling log under a mallet blow is a serious hazard.
Keep hands away from the blade path. The froe blade drops suddenly when the split opens; fingers on the log in the blade path will be cut.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
The froe

The froe has an L-shaped profile: a flat blade 20 to 30 cm long with a bevelled cutting edge, and a handle set at right angles to the blade. The handle is the lever. The blade is driven into the wood by striking the spine with a beetle mallet; then the handle is levered to open the split.
Setting up

Stand the log section on the chopping block, end grain up. Read the end grain for any checks (radial cracks from the drying process) or knots. Avoid splitting through a knot; position the froe to one side of any knot.
The technique
Position the froe blade on the end grain at the intended split line. Hold the handle vertical and the blade flat on the end grain.
Strike the spine of the froe with the beetle mallet two or three times to drive the blade 2 to 3 cm into the end grain.
Once the blade is seated, lever the froe handle toward one side to open the split. The split will run ahead of the blade and down the length of the log.

If the split runs off to one side (following a wave in the grain), lever in the opposite direction to steer it back. Lever gently: too much force causes the split to run to the far face before it reaches the bottom.
Once the two halves are separated, the froe withdraws easily from the open kerf.
The rule of halves

Always rive by halves. Split the full round into two halves, then each half into quarters, then each quarter into eighths, and so on until the pieces are the size needed. Never try to rive a thin sliver from the edge of a large piece: the thin sliver has less resistance than the large piece and the split will run into the large piece rather than following the intended line.
Species that rive well
Ash: the best all-round riving wood. Long, straight grain, very even splitting.
Sweet chestnut: rives along the rays; good for cleft fencing.
Oak rives cleanly along the medullary rays for flat work such as wattle weaving or shingles. For round-profile work, the rays cause the split to run unpredictably.
Hazel: rives predictably, especially for basket stakes.
Beech, sycamore: difficult to rive evenly due to interlocked grain. Better sawn for most purposes.
